Histology of respiratory
system Lab 2
Dr. Einas Yousef
eyousef@alfaisal.edu

Objectives
• Identify different components of the lung (bronchi, bronchiole, alveolar duct and
alveolar sac, and alveoli)
• Identify different layers forming the wall of different parts of the lung.
• Identify different cells lining the bronchi, bronchiole, alveolar duct and sac, alveoli.
• Differentiate between bronchi and bronchioles (epithelium, muscle and cartilage).
• Identify the epithelial lining and connective tissue forming the pleura.
• Correlate the structure and functions of different cells and components of the
respiratory tract (covered in lectures).

Mammal Trachea (c.s.)
Cross
section
in
trachea
and
esophagus
showing C-shaped hyaline cartilages in tracheal
wall that provide flexibility to the trachea and
maintains patency of the lumen. The open ends
of
the
cartilage
ring
are
on
the
posterior
surface,
against
the
esophagus.
They
are
bridged
by
a
bundle
of
smooth
muscle
(trachealis muscle) and a sheet of fibroelastic
tissue attached to the perichondrium. Some
seromucous acini are also present.
(Below) Transverse section (TS) showing four
layers forming the tracheal wall, from inside out
as following:
1) Mucosa: respiratory epithelium and lamina
propria
2) Submucosa: Loose connective tissue with
blood
and
lymphatic
vessels
and
seromucous acini.
3) Cartilaginous layer: hyaline cartilages.

Human lung (Intrapulmonary bronchi)
The intrapulmonary bronchi have the same general histologic
structure as the trachea with two changes:
The cartilage rings are replaced by hyaline cartilage (HC) plates
of irregular shape, around the entire circumference of the wall.
Addition
of
smooth
muscle
(SM)
to
form
a
complete
circumferential layer.

Intrapulmonary bronchus
The
wall
of
intrapulmonary
bronchi
is
composed of:
1. Mucosa: folded due to contraction of smooth
muscle in the wall.

Epithelium (E): pseudostratified epithelium.

Lamina propria (LP): loose connective tissue.
2. Muscularis:

A continuous layer of smooth muscle (SM) in
large bronchi.

More attenuated and loosely organized in
smaller bronchi.

Regulates the diameter of the airway.
3. Submucosa: loose connective tissue. Glands
are present in the larger bronchi.
4. Cartilage layer: discontinuous hyaline cartilage
(HC)
plates
that
become
smaller
as
the
bronchial diameter diminishes.
5. Adventitia is
moderately
dense
connective
tissue that is continuous with that of adjacent
structures.
LP

Bronchiole
The wall of bronchioles is composed of:
1.
Mucosa:
Epithelium: Large bronchioles have a ciliated,
pseudostratified columnar epithelium with few
goblet cells. Smaller bronchioles are lined by
simple ciliated columnar or cuboidal epithelium.
Club
(Clara)
cells
are
present
in
small
bronchioles,
and
their
numbers
are
greatly
increased along the length of the bronchioles.
lamina propria: loose connective tissue with
many elastic fibers.
2. Muscularis: A relatively thick layer of smooth
muscle (SM) is present in the wall of all
bronchioles.
3. Adventitia: Connective tissue, attached to the
surrounding alveoli.
Bronchioles are air-conducting ducts that measure 1 mm or
less in diameter. Large bronchioles branch repeatedly, giving
rise
to
the
smaller
terminal
bronchioles.
The
terminal
bronchioles branch to give rise to the respiratory bronchioles.
Cartilage plates and glands are not present in bronchioles.

Respiratory bronchiole
Respiratory bronchioles composed of areas lined with
simple cuboidal epithelium (E) (ciliated cells and club
cells). Smooth muscle (SM) bundles and elastic fibers
are present. Other areas composed of alveoli (lined by
very thin epithelium). Each respiratory bronchiole
branches into several alveolar ducts.

Alveolar duct and alveolar sac
• Alveolar ducts (AD) are elongated airways that have almost no walls, only alveoli (lined with very thin epithelium),
as their peripheral boundary. Rings of smooth muscle are present in the knob-like interalveolar septa.
• Alveolar sacs are spaces surrounded by clusters of alveoli. Alveolar sacs usually occur at the termination of an
alveolar duct but may occurs anywhere along its length.

Alveoli
Alveoli are terminal air spaces of the
respiratory system, where the gas
exchange occurs between the air and
the blood.
Each
alveolus
is
a
thin-walled
polyhedral chamber around 0.2 mm in
diameter.
Each alveolus is surrounded by a
network of capillaries (c) that brings
blood close to inhaled air inside the
alveolus.
Cells that can be detected in alveoli
are:
1. Type I pneumocytes (1).
2. Type II pneumocytes (2).

Visceral pleura
Visceral
pleura:
is
a
serous
membrane that tightly covers the
outer surface of each lung. it is
composed of:
1.
Simple
squamous
mesothelial
cells
(arrows).
Mesothelium produces thin film of
serous
fluid
that
acts
as
a
lubricant,
facilitating
smooth
sliding of one surface over the
other
during
respiratory
movement.
2. A thin connective tissue layer
containing collagen and elastic
fibers.
This
connective
tissue
connects the pleura to the lung
parenchyma
and
allows
for
flexibility during breathing.
